IVFellow Ugandans, friends, and partners,
The Government of Uganda is determined to achieve 
our goal of transforming Uganda from a peasant 
economy into a modern and prosperous country. It is 
what we must do to secure the future of our people. 
Our Vision 2040 and the Fourth National Development 
Plan (NDP IV) give us the road map: create jobs, raise 
household incomes, build industries, protect our 
environment, and ensure peace and stability.
The Cooperation Framework between the Government 
of Uganda and the United Nations is one of the 
instruments to help us move faster along that road. 
It aligns with our national plan and Africa’s Agenda 
2063, and it addresses the critical areas where we 
need real transformation: food systems, education, 
jobs and social protection, energy, climate resilience, 
and governance. These are the levers to unlock the 
ten-fold growth strategy and to make sure our young 
population becomes a source of wealth.
I want to emphasize the Parish Development Model 
(PDM). This is not a theory; it is practical economics. 
We are moving money and decision-making closer to 
the people. Every parish is a unit of wealth creation. 
With the support of our partners, including the UN, 
we shall bring services, credit, and markets directly 
to the households still stuck in subsistence. By 2030, 
we must have shifted millions of our people into 
the money economy. That is when we shall see real 
prosperity.
This Framework is not about government alone, nor 
about the UN alone. It is about all of us - citizens, civil 
society, private sector, academia, and development 
partners - working under one national plan, with one 
vision. When you work together, you avoid duplication, 
you save resources, and you achieve faster. Even 
in my village, when people dig a trench together, the 
work finishes quickly, and the results are visible. 
Development is the same.
I commend the United Nations Country Team for 
aligning their work with our priorities. I call on all 
actors to rally behind the NDP IV and the PDM. Let us 
remain focused, disciplined, and innovative. Uganda is 
not poor; it is rich in people, land, and opportunities. 
With the right organization, institutions and people 
we shall achieve inclusive growth, protect our 
environment, and secure the future for generations
to come.
H.E General Yoweri Kaguta Museveni
President of the Republic of Uganda

VIII
Uganda and the United Nations have worked side by side 
to advance our shared vision for development. Guided 
by Vision 2040, the National Development Plans, and the 
2030 Agenda and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), 
we have made tangible progress. Uganda has risen to 
medium human development status, fulfilled two of three 
criteria for graduation from the Least Developed Countries 
category, and reduced maternal and child mortality. We 
have advanced social protection, promoted gender equality, 
and built stronger food and energy systems. The Parish 
Development Model is bringing services and financing closer 
to households, while Uganda’s progressive refugee policy 
remains a model for the world, and our role in promoting 
regional peace and stability continues to be recognized. 
These are results of working together, with government 
leadership, citizen effort, and partner support. 
The Government of Uganda and the UN system are proud of 
the achievements we have registered together over the past 
five years, through Ministries, Departments and Agencies 
working hand-in-hand with 29 UN entities bringing diverse 
skills and mandates to Uganda’s development. Looking 
forward, the Pact for the Future provides a powerful platform 
for developing countries like Uganda. Uganda has already 
shown leadership in shaping its outcomes, and the UN will 
continue to back the Government to translate the Pact into 
tangible gains for Ugandans. Our priorities remain clear: 
better collaboration, nimbler and more efficient operations, 
and stronger partnerships that serve people.
The years ahead hold even greater promise. Hosting the 
NAM and G77 Summits, the Africa Regional Forum on 
Sustainable Development, and the Africa Cup of Nations 
(AFCON) 2027 will place Uganda at the centre of continental 
and global attention. These milestones create opportunities 
to attract investment, expand trade, boost tourism, and 
showcase Uganda’s resilience and ambition. At the global 
level, dialogues on financing, debt, climate, and the Pact for 
the Future open space for Uganda to influence and benefit 
from reforms. With the Cooperation Framework 2026–2030 
built around the NDP IV and the Parish Development Model, 
we now have a joint roadmap to turn these opportunities 
into real gains for all Ugandans.
We reaffirm our commitment to enhanced coordination 
through mobilizing and convening all stakeholders to actively 
contribute to Uganda’s transformation coherently, efficiently 
and effectively.The Government, through the Office of the 
Prime Minister, reaffirms its leadership in coordinating SDG 
implementation and national development efforts. The 
United Nations, through the Resident Coordinator, commits 
to mobilizing the full weight of the UN system, local, regional, 
and global, to back Uganda’s aspirations, from climate-smart 
livelihoods to food systems, energy, and governance. But to 
succeed, we must all change how we work. Businesses as 
usual will not deliver the ten-fold growth strategy or high 
middle-income status by 2040. Business unusual, driven by 
urgency, discipline, and innovation, is the way forward. Our 
call is to every actor, government, citizens, private sector, 
civil society, and partners: let us rally behind one national 
plan, work as one, and ensure Uganda’s next chapter is 
defined by inclusive growth, resilience, and prosperity for all.

The United Nations Sustainable Development Framework (UNSDCF) articulates the United Nations’ collective 
response to support the Government of Uganda in addressing national priorities and gaps in their pathway 
towards meeting NDP IV, Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets and National Vision aspirations. The 
Cooperation Framework is a vehicle for supporting development and social transformation; offering options to 
reframe economic policies and practices around sustainability for inclusive, diversified and job-intensive economic 
development, and promoting access to and utilization of basic social and protection services that advances human 
rights and well-being of people in Uganda, and protecting the planet. The Cooperation Framework also promotes 
the spirit of partnerships that is at the core of the 2030 Agenda. The Cooperation Framework tailors responses to 
national priorities ensuring that all United Nations entities can effectively support national implementation of the 
2030 Agenda. By signing hereunder, the participating parties endorse the UNSDCF 2026-2030.

XVI
Uganda has made steady progress toward the 2030 Agenda; 
evidenced by increased resilience of the economy to both 
domestic and external shocks. Economic growth has remained 
robust, reaching 6.3 per cent in 2024/25 and projected to rise 
to 7 per cent in 2025/26, supported by gains in agriculture, 
industry, and an expected boost from oil and gas. The 
Country’s role in the region remains strong, with leadership in 
peacekeeping, refugee hosting, and South–South cooperation. 
Uganda has made important progress on the Sustainable 
Development Goals (SDGs), with reductions in poverty, 
maternal and child mortality, and stunting in children, as 
well as improvements in education enrolment and access 
to health services. The country has moved into the medium 
human development category, with a Human Development 
Index score of 0.582, and met two of the three criteria for 
Least Developed Country graduation. The Fourth National 
Development Plan (NDP IV), in line with Vision 2040 and the 
Ten-fold economic growth, provides strategic direction for 
the next five years. Opportunities for accelerated progress 
lie in agro-industrialization, tourism especially in view of the 
2027 Africa Cup of Nations football tournament co-hosted 
with Tanzania and Kenya. These are also immense potential 
in mineral and mining development, science and innovation, 
digital expansion and regional integration which collectively 
provide for productivity, employment generation, value addition 
and accelerated socio-economic progress. 
These gains are suppressed by structural challenges holding 
back Uganda’s full development potential. Inequalities persist 
between rural and urban areas, and multidimensional poverty 
still affects 42 per cent of the population (UBOS, 2022). 
Uganda’s youthful population with three quarters under the age 
of 30 offers a potential demographic dividend but undermined 
by high youth unemployment and skills gap. Further challenges 
include gender disparities, poor learning outcomes and rising 
skills mismatches. 
Although Uganda has made progress on key human 
development indicators, it is yet to reach the income threshold 
for middle-income status. Environmental degradation and 
climate shocks pose increasing threats to livelihoods, while 
issues of weak governance, limited accountability, shrinking 
civic space, and uneven service delivery continue to erode 
public trust. In addition, the country faces emerging security 
threats, including terrorism and violent extremism, underscoring 
the need for prevention and resilience-building in national 
development strategies.
The UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 
(2026–2030), or Cooperation Framework (Cooperation 
Framework), is the central instrument guiding UN engagement 
in Uganda. It is guided by national leadership; aligned with NDP 
IV, Agenda 2063 and the 2030 Agenda; and shaped by inclusive 
consultations with the Government, civil society, the private 
sector and vulnerable groups. The Cooperation Framework 
responds to structural challenges – weak governance, 
climate risk, inequality, fragility, and rapid urbanization – while 
identifying opportunities to accelerate progress through the 
six SDG transitions: (1) food systems, (2) energy access and 
affordability, (3) digital connectivity, (4) education; (5) jobs and 
social protection and (6) climate change, biodiversity loss and 
pollution. 
The Cooperation Framework is structured around three 
strategic priorities: (i) Transformative and Inclusive Human 
Development, (ii) Sustainable Ecosystems and Climate-Smart 
Development and (iii) Integrated, Inclusive and Rights-Based 
Governance. Together, these priorities reflect the commitment 
to leaving no one behind and dismantling systemic barriers 
to inclusion. The Cooperation Framework narrows its focus 
to catalytic areas with the greatest potential to transform 
systems, including food systems, education, energy, green 
and decent jobs for youth, gender, social protection and digital 
governance. These areas are the engines to turbocharge wider 
socioeconomic shifts and address Uganda’s demographic and 
structural challenges. Gender equality, human rights and childfocused outcomes are integrated across all results.

UGANDA | UNITED NATIONS SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT COOPERATION FRAMEWORK 2026-2030The Cooperation Framework is designed to drive 
meaningful system changes. It will reshape how the UN 
works in Uganda, building stronger collaboration around 
shared priorities with the Government and partners. 
It aligns reforms in human development, governance 
and climate-smart growth, bringing all actors under one 
national plan and shifting how institutions deliver for 
citizens. Reflecting the UN reform agenda, it seeks to 
simplify procedures, reduce duplication and increase 
efficiency. Strategically tied to the Pact for the Future, it 
aims to deliver results in new ways and embed lasting 
change.
The theory of change distinguishes what can be achieved 
within the Cooperation Framework’s five-year span from 
the longer-term impacts of Vision 2040. Intermediate 
outcomes are streamlined to show progress by 2030. 
The core logic is clear: if Uganda advances human 
development, builds climate-smart and sustainable 
entrepreneur and natural ecosystems, and pursues 
inclusive and rights-based governance, then it will 
accelerate its transition towards being a more inclusive, 
resilient and prosperous middle-income country. 
Geographically, the Cooperation Framework prioritizes 
vulnerable regions, such as West Nile, Northern Uganda, 
Karamoja and climate-vulnerable areas. 
The UN’s comparative advantage lies in its normative 
mandate, neutrality and convening power. It adds value 
in advancing human rights and governance, linking 
humanitarian and development action, supporting 
refugee inclusion and bringing global expertise in health, 
education, food systems and climate resilience. The 
UN’s contribution to implementing the Cooperation 
Framework is centred on catalytic areas that can shift 
systems – transformative education, food systems, 
climate resilience, gender equality, digital inclusion and 
governance reform.
Delivery will be through 32 UN entities, both resident and 
non-resident, working together under the UN Country 
Team configuration. This country team includes funds, 
programmes, specialized agencies and new partners 
such as the International Telecommunication Union, UN 
Office of Counter-Terrorism and the UN Office for Digital 
and Emerging Technologies. Their combined technical 
expertise and mandates will support integrated solutions, 
joint programming and agile responses to Uganda’s 
evolving priorities.
Implementation will rely on joint workplans, common 
programming instruments and the Business Operations 
Strategy. A Joint Steering Committee will provide 
strong Government-UN accountability, while internal 
UN structures will enhance coherence across agencies. 
Financing will be mobilized through the Integrated 
National Financing Framework, pooled mechanisms and 
partnerships with international financial institutions, the 
private sector and non-traditional investors. Efforts will 
also draw on South-South and triangular cooperation, 
climate finance and innovative approaches such as digital 
platforms for resource mobilization. Partnerships with 
civil society, academia and local authorities will ensure 
inclusion, while strong communications on results will 
sustain trust and visibility.
The Cooperation Framework is underpinned by a 
monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) plan that 
uses nationally aligned indicators and disaggregated 
data to capture inequalities. Progress will be tracked 
through regular reviews and annual reporting, with a 
midterm review to inform adaptation to shifting contexts. 
The MEL plan reinforces accountability, adaptability 
and learning, ensuring that the Cooperation Framework 
remains responsive to Uganda’s needs. Identified risks 
include fiscal pressures, funding cuts, regional instability 
and climate shocks, while assumptions rest on political 
stability and sustained commitment to reform. 
This Cooperation Framework is not business as usual. 
It is designed to drive system change – bringing 
the UN together as one, aligning fully with Uganda’s 
development agenda and embedding equity, resilience 
and sustainability into national systems. It reflects 
the reform momentum of UN 2.0 and the Pact for the 
Future by simplifying procedures, cutting overlaps and 
mobilizing collective action. With Uganda’s youthful 
population and growth potential, the next five years 
offer a critical window to deliver transformative results. 
The Cooperation Framework is the shared road map for 
Uganda and the UN to work together towards an inclusive, 
prosperous and sustainable future.

1.1 Country Context
Uganda is a young and fast-growing country at the heart 
of East Africa, with a dynamic population and a strong 
regional role. The United Nations works with Government 
and partners through the Resident Coordinator’s Office 
and the UN Country Team to advance national priorities and 
the SDGs. This section sets the context for the Cooperation 
Framework. It gives a clear picture of the economy, human 
development, demographics, climate and environment, 
governance, and regional dynamics. It highlights progress 
and gaps in achieving the Sustainable development Goals 
(SDGs) by 2030, risks and opportunities, and what they 
mean for Uganda’s long-term development. It also shows 
how these trends align with Vision 2040, Fourth National 
Development Plan (NDP IV), Agenda 2063 and the SDGs, 
and how they shape the UN’s support. 
Uganda’s economy has continued to show resilience, 
defying projections and rising steadily since all COVID-19 
measures were removed in 2022. But disparities in 
economic gains and outcomes remain stark. In FY2024/25, 
real GDP growth reached 6.3 per cent, slightly higher than 
the 6.1 per cent registered in FY2023/24, reflecting postCOVID recovery and improved external demand. GDP 
per capita was recorded at USD 1,146. In the FY2024/25, 
the agricultural and industrial sectors continued to post 
strong growth, growing by 7.2 per cent and 8.4 per cent, 
respectively. Improved food crop production particularly 
bananas, maize, and beans – was key to the sector’s 
performance. In the industrial sector, robust manufacturing 
growth was led by the pharmaceutical sector, followed by 
increased value addition in construction. The services 
sector continues to drive growth, especially on information 
and communication technology, contributing 43.1 per cent 
to GDP in FY 2023/24.
Uganda’s public debt reached USD 29.1 billion by end 2024, 
projected to rise to USD 31.5 billion (UGX 116 trillion) by 
June 2025. According to the 2025 Budget Speech, debt 
is now 51.3 per cent of GDP, consistent with the charter 
of fiscal responsibility but exceed which now exceeds 
the International Monetary Fund threshold recommended 
thresholds for low income countries. Debt servicing 
already consumes 32 shillings of every 100 collected in 
revenue, crowding out social spending and weakening 
public confidence in fiscal management. Government 
is responding through domestic revenue mobilisation, 
concessional borrowing, and digital financial platforms 
to broaden participation in government securities. While

this will demand double-digit growth, a higher tax-to-GDP

expanding infrastructure, promoting science and technology, 
deepening industrialization, and protecting the environment.

this transformation.

Poverty declined modestly, with monetary poverty falling

subsistence households into the money economy by

SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth). However, 
income disparities remain, particularly between urban 
and rural areas, and multidimensional poverty affects

50 per cent. This pathway will rely on four growth drivers: 
agro-industrialization, tourism development, mineralbased industrialization (including oil and gas), and science, 
technology, and innovation - collectively referred to as the 
ATMS sectors.
Uganda’s vision is fully aligned with global and continental 
goals. The SDGs and Agenda 2063 share Uganda’s priorities 
on inclusive growth, decent work, peace, good governance, 
sustainable resource use, resilient infrastructure, food 
security, gender equality, and climate action. The emphasis 
across all plans is to deliver growth that is inclusive, 
accountable, resilient, and leaves no one behind. The 
vision is premised on strong institutions, sound public 
financial management, capable governance systems, 
broad partnerships, and sustained investment in people. 
The Fourth National Development Plan (NDP IV), covering 
2025/26 to 2029/30, will guide delivery of Vision in this 
phase; to increase household incomes and create decent 
jobs, while driving sustainable industrialization, inclusive 
growth, and wealth creation. The plan recognizes the 
importance of effective governance, capable institutions, 
resilient service delivery systems, environmental protection, 
and the full participation of women, youth, refugees, and 
marginalized groups. NDP IV maintains alignment with the 
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Africa’s Agenda 
2063, placing global and continental aspirations in Uganda’s 
national priorities. The Cooperation Framework aligns 
directly with this vision, supporting Uganda to manage the 
transitions, address trade-offs, and maintain an inclusive 
development pathway that prioritizes people, institutions, 
and long-term resilience.

Over the past five years, collaboration and engagement 
between the United Nations and the Government of 
Uganda have deepened, leading to a more strategic, 
integrated and forward-looking partnership. The United 
Nations further aligned its support with national priorities 
and there has been strengthened joint planning and joint 
advocacy through institutional mechanisms, as well as 
a shift towards more joint programme implementation 
and systems-level support. Collaboration has expanded 
into emerging areas, such as digitization, innovation 
and sustainable financing, and it has deepened in crisis 
response and resilience-building, especially in the refugee 
programme. The partnership emphasizes inclusive 
dialogue, improved data systems and a two-agenda-oneprogramme1
 approach to accelerating the achievement 
of the SDGs and Africa Agenda 2063. These changes 
reflect a shift towards more agile and transformative 
cooperation.
The UN system’s value lies in its global normative 
mandate and its neutrality and convening power. It brings 
comparative advantages in advancing human rights and 
humanitarian–development–peace linkages and in its 
technical expertise in health, education, food systems 
and climate resilience. The Cooperation Framework 
(Cooperation Framework) builds on the United Nations’ 
comparative advantage by aligning engagement to areas 
where it adds unique value: reaching underserved regions, 
mobilizing inclusive partnerships and anchoring results 
in global standards while supporting Uganda’s national 
priorities.

2.1 From Country Analysis to Cooperation Framework
The UN Sustainable Development Cooperation 
Framework 2026–2030 is the central instrument guiding 
the partnership between the United Nations and the 
Government of Uganda over the next five years. It sets 
out shared priorities to turbocharge progress towards 
the SDGs, aligned with Vision 2040 and NDP IV. Informed 
by data, foresight and inclusive consultations, the 
Cooperation Framework reflects a renewed commitment 
to deliver tangible results for people and the planet. It is 
grounded in national leadership and global commitments, 
including the six transitions of the 2030 Agenda, Agenda 
2063 and the Pact for the Future. 
The Cooperation Framework brings together the full 
UN system in Uganda to support integrated, peoplecentred solutions that respond to Uganda’s evolving 
development context. The design process was co-led 
with the Government and actively involved UN entities, 
including non-resident agencies, regional commissions 
and specialized agencies. Consultations extended to 
development partners, academia, women’s rights civil 
society organizations (CSOs), youth networks, childfocused organizations and groups representing the 
interests of people with disabilities. Innovative methods, 
such as the integration of these groups into all smaller 
discussion groups and co-chairing of dialogues, ensured 
voices of underserved groups were heard and integrated.

Environmental degradation, deforestation,

Rapid population growth and unplanned

urbanization, if well-managed, can be a 
driver of innovation and growth. Uganda 
has the chance to reimagine urban 
development through smart cities,

Social and Cultural 
Norms Reinforcing 
Exclusion
Entrenched norms continue to exclude 
women, persons with disabilities, refugees, 
and other marginalized groups from public 
life, service access, and decision-making. 
Investing in rights-based approaches, 
gender-responsive laws, and community

to build a more equal and inclusive 
society.
Forced 
Displacement and 
Regional Instability
As a major refugee-hosting country, 
Uganda faces stress on services and

Opportunities exist in localized solutions

plans, strengthening migration 
governance, and leveraging regional 
cooperation to address root causes.
Education System 
Misalignment
Uganda’s education system struggles 
with access, quality, and relevance. 
High dropout rates and poor learning 
outcomes, especially for girls and rural 
youth, limit prospects for decent work and 
inclusive growth. Transforming education 
through digital tools, vocational 
pathways, and inclusive curricula can 
equip young people to thrive in a fastchanging world.

challenges and Weak

despite Uganda’s agricultural potential.

triple dividend for health, food security, 
and economic growth.

Sector Synergy

and private sectors constrains Uganda’s 
development potential. Mismatched 
priorities, lack of trust, and regulatory 
bottlenecks limit innovation and 
investment. Strengthening public-private 
dialogue, streamlining regulations, 
and developing blended financing 
mechanisms can unleash Uganda’s 
entrepreneurial potential and deliver

and Digital Deficit
Weak infrastructure especially in 
transport, energy, and ICT limits

expanding access to basic services,

livelihoods in underserved areas.

142.2 The UN’s Strategic Role and Positioning
The UN system in Uganda is strategically positioned to 
support the country’s development transitions by leveraging 
its normative mandate, global expertise and convening power. 
Through this Cooperation Framework, the UN will support 
Uganda in achieving six systemic transitions: inclusive 
growth, resilient food systems, universal health coverage, 
climate action, digital transformation and strengthened 
institutions. The goals of the Cooperation Framework 
priorities are to support the Tenfold Growth Strategy and 
sustained wealth creation, sustainable industrialization, full 
economic monetization and robust private sector growth in 
which the private sector is profoundly involved in domestic 
resources, blended finance and private capital mobilization.
The UN adds value where it is most needed – advancing human 
rights, governance and accountability; linking humanitarian, 
development and peace work; bringing technical expertise in 
health, education, climate and food systems; and serving as a 
trusted convener of governments – national, sub-national and 
local, civil society, private sector and development partners. It 
also brings expertise in preventing and countering terrorism 
and violent extremism, ensuring these efforts are rightsbased, inclusive and integrated within broader governance 
and resilience programmes. It also promotes South-South 
cooperation and knowledge exchange, drawing on regional 
and global experience.
The Cooperation Framework concentrates efforts in the 
most vulnerable regions as articulated in the Country 
Analysis –West Nile, Northern Uganda, Karamoja and 
climate vulnerable areas – while prioritizing youth, 
women, refugees, children, people with disabilities, and 
refugee-hosting communities. The United Nations will 
mobilize resources by aligning donor contributions to joint 
programmes and pooled mechanisms, while expanding 
opportunities for private and multilateral financing.
Internally, the UN will work as one system, planning, 
implementing and speaking with a single voice. Externally, 
it will continue to advocate for rights, equality, climate action 
and resilience, acting as the voice of those most at risk, while 
remaining in close partnership with the Government. The 
Cooperation Framework is designed to remain agile, able to 
pivot between humanitarian and development action and to 
anticipate risks, such as economic shocks, epidemics and 
climate disasters. This approach strengthens relevance, 
credibility and coherence across all national systems including 
those of the UN. It also enables the UN to make measurable 
contributions to governance, livelihoods, human capital and 
resilience, deepen joint UN-Government accountability, expand 
resource mobilization opportunities and communicate results 
more effectively to sustain impact nd trust.
2.3 Theory of Change for the Cooperation Framework Priorities
This theory of change outlines how the Government 
of Uganda and the United Nations system, together 
with key counterparts. including the Africa Union 
Development Agency, international financial institutions, 
local and external development partners, CSOs and 
the private sector, will work together to accelerate 
inclusive, equitable and sustainable development over 
the period 2026 to 2030. It serves as a shared blueprint 
and articulates the collective understanding of how 
development change can happen in Uganda. It will serve 
as a compass, guiding joint efforts towards achieving 
the national aspirations articulated in Vision 2040 and 
NDP IV as well as the 2030 Agenda, Doha Programme 
of Action for Least Developed Countries, Awaza 
Programme of Action for Landlocked Least Developed 
Countries, the East Africa Community Vision 2050 and 
the African Union Agenda 2063.
The Cooperation Framework is designed to bring a 
meaningful system change. It will shift how the UN 
works and prioritizes more collaboration around shared 
priorities with the Government and partners. It will 
link reforms in human development, governance and 
climate-smart growth; rallying people around one plan 
– the National Development Plan; and change how 
institutions work with and for citizens. It reflects the 
recent reform agenda by cutting overlaps, simplifying 
procedures and improving efficiency. Aligned with the 
Pact for the Future, it is designed to deliver results 
differently and drive lasting system change.
The Cooperation Framework is built on three 
interconnected strategic priorities: (i) Transformative 
and Inclusive Human Development, (ii) Sustainable 
Ecosystems and Climate-smart Development, and (iii) 
Integrated, Inclusive and Rights-based Governance. These 
priorities reflect a shared commitment to leaving no one 
behind and to removing systemic barriers that reinforce 
exclusion. They narrow the focus of the Cooperation 
Framework to catalytic areas with the highest potential 
for impact, such as food systems transformation, 
transformative education, energy, green and decent jobs 
for youth, social projection and automated governance 
systems. These areas were selected because they trigger 
wider socioeconomic transformation and directly address 
Uganda’s demographic and structural challenges. Gender 
and child-specific targets will be embedded across 
outcomes to ensure inclusivity.
The Cooperation Framework is built around six outcomes 
framed around the five Ps (People, Prosperity, Planet, 
Peace and Partnership).
There is an outcome on gender and disability that 
emphasizes the United Nation’s commitment to leaving 
no one behind (See Figure 5 above for the Cooperation 
Framework Outcomes). The theory of change 
distinguishes between Cooperation Framework outcomes 
achievable by 2030 and longer-term impacts aligned to 
Vision 2040. Intermediate outcomes are simplified to 
reflect progress within the Cooperation Framework’s fiveyear period, ensuring a realistic results chain. 
The theory of change espouses a central 
logic that states that:
IF  Uganda simultaneously advances and transforms 
human development, fosters sustainable ecosystems 
and climate-smart development, and pursues integrated, 
inclusive and right-based governance systems, 
THEN  it will accelerate its transition towards a more 
inclusive, prosperous and resilient middle-income 
country by 2030.

182.3.1 Transformative and Inclusive Human 
Development (People and Prosperity)
Uganda’s investments in human capital will translate 
into improved quality and coverage of education, health, 
nutrition, social protection, and water and sanitation 
services. This will be achieved through stronger public 
systems, improved financing, better data use and 
expanded delivery capacity at national and sub-national 
levels. Social sector reforms will prioritize underserved 
regions and vulnerable populations, including women, 
youth and people with disabilities. The Cooperation 
Framework reflects Uganda’s obligations under the 
Convention on the Rights of the Child, Convention on the 
Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women 
(CEDAW) and the Convention on the Rights of Persons 
with Disabilities (CRPD). It addresses early childhood 
development, malnutrition, child participation, protection 
from violence, and child-focused budgeting. These 
priorities will be mainstreamed across all outcomes, 
ensuring that children’s rights and vulnerabilities 
are explicitly considered in policies, systems and
investments.
In line with the six transitions for SDG acceleration, 
transformative education, food systems, jobs and social 
protection will turbocharge the achievement of targets 
under this people and prosperity strategic priority. Strategic 
investments and targeted support will benefit youth, women, 
female-headed households and micro, small and mediumsized enterprises (MSMEs) with a focus on enterprise 
development, skills enhancement and financial inclusion. 
Energy access, climate-smart agriculture and waste 
management will be explicitly framed as part of Uganda’s 
food systems transformation. This approach highlights the 
interlinkages between production, environment, nutrition 
and livelihoods to ensure interventions are coherent and 
address systemic barriers to food security and resilience. 
Interventions will prioritize high-potential sectors such 
as agriculture, tourism, mineral development, digital and 
emerging technologies and innovation ecosystems, thereby 
expanding opportunities for decent work, entrepreneurship 
and inclusive economic transformation. Job creation and 
social protection are high on the agenda of the Government 
and its partners. The UN will strengthen the alignment 
between education, skills development and employment 
opportunities. The UN will also support the enforcement 
of existing policies and regulations to raise the quality of 
learning and skilling programmes. 
Uganda continues to face low pre-primary enrolment 
and higher levels of school dropout and out-of-school 
children than other countries in the Eastern and Southern 
Africa region. The UN will back the implementation 
of the National Childhood Care and Education Policy, 
the Inclusive Education Strategy and the Digital 
Agenda Strategy. Institutional support will target skills 
development authorities, technical and vocational 
education and training providers, and key actors in 
the informal sector to ensure that more individuals, 
particularly young people and women, have the right skill 
set to access the contemporary job market and have 
decent and sustainable work. Uganda’s long-term growth 
depends on harnessing its full demographic dividend 
by investing in education, health and job creation for 
its rapidly growing youthful population. For youth not 
in education, employment or training (NEET), the UN 
will engage with partners to design and adopt multiple 
flexible pathways to increase young people’s access 
to skilling opportunities and support their transition to
earning. 
Achieving Uganda’s ambition of tenfold economic 
growth and social transformation by 2040 will require 
addressing deep-rooted structural dualism in the 
economy. The sharp divide between high-paying, 
high-skilled formal employment and the widespread 
prevalence of low-incomes and informality highlights 
the urgency of formalizing the informal sector. The UN 
will support targeted reforms that promote inclusive 
enterprise development, strengthen regulatory 
and legal frameworks and that expand access to 
finance, markets and social protection for informal
workers. 
Tackling informality must also go together with reducing 
inequalities by confronting the social and cultural 
norms that perpetuate discrimination. Integrated policy, 
advocacy and accountability mechanisms will be 
employed to combat gender-based violence, harmful 
practices and the exclusion of persons with disabilities. 
This approach will foster an enabling environment for 
inclusive human development, anchored in strong local 
leadership and meaningful citizen participation. Food 
systems remain a major enabler of these outcomes 
under this strategic priority. Uganda can accelerate 
food systems transformation by investing in climatesmart agriculture, strengthening agricultural value 
chains and ensuring smallholder farmers, especially 
women and youth, have access to markets, finance 
and technology. The UN will reinforce these efforts 
by providing policy support, mobilizing resources and 
fostering innovation and partnerships that make the 
country’s food systems more inclusive, resilient and
sustainable. ‘Strategic investments in the health 
sector, the development of resilient health systems, and 
enhanced multisectoral collaboration in health service 
delivery are critical drivers of increased workforce 
productivity, longer life expectancy, and improved quality 
of life, ultimately fostering sustainable socio-economic 
development.
2.3.2 Sustainable Ecosystems and Climate-Smart 
Development (Planet)
Uganda will strengthen its capacity to manage land, 
forests, water and other natural resources in a way that 
is sustainable and equitable. This will require stronger 
regulatory frameworks, effective land-use planning and 
enhanced environmental monitoring. National and district 
institutions will be supported to enforce laws, adopt climatesmart planning tools and engage local communities in 
managing and protecting their resources. A focus will be 
placed on strengthening local government capacity, so 
that decision-making is closer to the people and directly 
responsive to environmental challenges they face. Targeted 
actions will promote clean energy access, circular 
economy models and climate-smart agriculture, while 
creating opportunities for decent green jobs. Investments 
in adaptation, ecosystem restoration and disaster risk 
reduction will be scaled up, with special attention given 
to fragile ecosystems, high-risk areas and the needs of 
displaced populations and host communities in climatevulnerable zones. This work will reinforce the energy 
transition, reduce dependency on unsustainable practices 
and unlock innovation for affordable renewable energy 
solutions.
Greater emphasis will be placed on addressing the social 
determinants of health that influence population wellbeing and contribute to health inequities. The United 
Nations will advocate for strategic investments targeting 
the social, economic, commercial, and environmental 
factors that shape health outcomes. This will be achieved 
through multi-sectoral and intersectoral collaboration, 
active engagement of local governments, individuals and 
communities, and strengthened governance of health 
systems. These will be aimed at enhancing system 
performance, resilience, and sustainability, ultimately 
leading to improved population health.
Progress will depend on integrated approaches that 
link agriculture, energy, environment and livelihoods. 
A systems approach will connect food systems 
transformation to sustainable land and water use, align 
the digital transition to real-time environmental monitoring 
and early warning systems, and support education 
reforms that build the skills needed for a green economy. 
Coordination will extend across sectors and actors, with 
data-driven decision-making and innovative financing, 
such as climate funds, blended finance and public-private 
partnerships, reinforcing Uganda’s transition to climatesmart development.
Implementation of the Cooperation Framework will 
also address the broader social protection and jobs 
transition by ensuring that climate action generates 
inclusive economic opportunities, especially for 
women, youth and people with disabilities. This will be 
matched with transformative governance reforms that 
embed environmental accountability, ensure citizen 
participation and strengthen institutional transparency. 
These shifts will reduce the structural inequalities 
that leave communities most exposed to climate
risks.
The transformative nature of this planet strategic priority 
lies in its ability to change how Uganda’s economic, social, 
political and environmental systems function; for example 
by integrating environmental concerns into economic 
planning, embedding resilience strengthening into social 
policies, aligning the aims of national institutions with 
global standards for climate action and putting gender 
issues at the heart of plans for climate change adaptation, 
disaster risks reduction and environmental sustainability. 
By linking environmental protection to livelihoods, energy 
security, education and governance, Uganda will not only 
build resilient communities and ecosystems but also 
position itself to benefit from global shifts towards green 
growth and low-carbon development.

202.3.3 Integrated, Inclusive and Rights-Based 
Governance (Peace and Partnership)
Strong, transparent and accountable institutions are 
essential for development results to last. Uganda will 
enhance the capacity of national and sub-national 
authorities to uphold rights, enforce laws and deliver 
services fairly. The focus will be on strengthening 
justice institutions, promoting inclusive and 
participatory planning and ensuring accountability 
across the public sector and NDP IV priority
programmes.
Interventions will continue to expand national and 
sub-national capacities for the implementation of 
development initiatives, improve civic space, enable 
citizen participation in governance and decision-making 
and build trust between communities and state actors. 
Special attention will go to youth engagement, inclusion 
of women, the role of the media and civil society’s 
contribution to development monitoring. Institutions will 
be supported to implement anti-corruption measures, 
address social grievances and promote peaceful 
coexistence and resilience for preventing violent 
extremism.
Partnerships will be deepened at all levels: sub-national, 
national, regional and global. Regional cooperation 
and global alliances will be fostered to support Uganda 
in responding to geopolitical uncertainties, climate 
change, cross-border conflicts, organized crime and 
refugee movements. The creation and capacitation of 
trade corridors will be facilitated so that Uganda can 
become a key trade and logistics hub in the region. Digital 
transformation and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to 
drive growth of smallholder farmers, agri-businesses and 
MSMEs will contribute to Uganda being able to export 
high-value goods. 
Uganda will adapt to a changing global order that is marked 
by multipolar politics using diplomacy, sound governance 
and partnerships to maintain a stable policy and enabling 
environment that guarantees long-term sustainable and 
transformative development for the country.

382.5 Cross-border, and regional cooperation
Uganda’s location in a region with economic hardship 
and multiple and diverse conflicts means it continues 
to host large numbers of refugees and migrants, mainly 
from Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan 
and the Democratic Republic of Congo. With over 1.9 
million refugees and asylum seekers, the pressure on the 
already limited resources and basic services in refugeehosting communities remains high. These regions face 
persistent insecurity, cross-border smuggling and weak 
infrastructure. Informal crossings outnumber formal ones 
and most official entry points are not adequately equipped. 
Border communities are often left behind in development 
efforts and remain vulnerable to trafficking, violence and 
rights violations. 
Uganda frequently experiences outbreaks of epidemicprone diseases such as Ebola, yellow fever, and polio, 
often linked to cross-border movements involving traders, 
families, refugees, and communities residing along shared 
borders. In response, the United Nations will collaborate 
with the Government of Uganda and neighboring countries 
to strengthen joint efforts in the prevention, control, and 
response to disease outbreaks triggered by cross-border 
activities.
The UN will work with the Government to strengthen 
cross-border governance, enhance cross-border trade, 
improve the use of border management information 
systems, ensure protection-sensitive approaches in 
refugee-hosting areas and enhance border resilience 
against exploitation by terrorist and criminal networks. It 
will support coordinated action by involving key actors to 
improve delivery service, uphold human rights, promote 
safe and regular migration, and address underlying drivers 
of forced displacement. Based on need, as evident in 
locations such as Rwenzori, Karamoja and the West Nile, 
the United Nations will continue to support early warning 
systems, social cohesion and local peacebuilding. Crossborder collaboration will also include efforts to prevent and 
counter terrorism and violent extremism, complementing 
existing African Union (AU), Intergovernmental Authority 
on Development (IGAD) and East Africa Community (EAC) 
mechanisms to address shared security challenges. These 
efforts will also focus on improving data, inter-agency 
coordination and institutional capacity at Uganda’s major 
border points. Through the Cooperation Framework, the 
UN entities in Uganda will explore a joint programme 
with the EAC on transboundary water management and 
cross-border trade facilitation, particularly benefiting 
refugees and small-scale agri-entrepreneurs. This builds 
on Uganda’s regional integration agenda and enhances 
resilience in border communities.
Uganda’s participation in regional economic blocs, such as 
the AfCFTA, EAC, COMESA and IGAD, presents significant 
opportunities for trade expansion, industrialization 
and inclusive economic growth. However, realizing 
these benefits requires overcoming several persistent 
challenges, including non-tariff barriers, regulatory 
inconsistencies and infrastructure connectivity gaps. 
To address this, the United Nations will provide targeted 
capacity-building support to both the Government 
and the private sector. This support will focus on 
implementing Uganda’s national AfCFTA strategy, 
enhancing compliance with regional trade agreements 
and strengthening cross-border governance and border 
management systems. Key areas of intervention will 
include enhancing MSME export readiness, developing 
and upgrading select commodity value chains, and 
addressing the trade finance gap particularly for youthand women-led enterprises. Additionally, efforts will be 
directed towards supporting the development of a robust 
digital infrastructure and supportive policy environment 
to facilitate the growth of e-commerce and digital trade.
2.6 Sustainability
The sustainability of results under this Cooperation 
Framework is built on national ownership and leadership. 
The Cooperation Framework was co-created with the 
Government and other national actors, with their inputs 
in both country analysis and the design of priorities, 
outcomes and outputs. All joint programmes and 
initiatives emerging from the framework will be designed 
and delivered using national systems wherever possible, 
placing national institutions at the centre of planning and 
implementation. This makes the Cooperation Framework 
a practical tool to advance Uganda’s development agenda, 
and not a parallel effort.
The Cooperation Framework draws from past lessons 
that emphasized the need for deeper institutional 
anchoring, stronger coordination and improved gender 
integration. It also responds to previous challenges of 
fragmented programming by consolidating outcomes 
and embedding robust MEL systems. These adjustments 
aim to ensure sustainability and accountability across 
all areas of work. The UN will work with the Government 
to strengthen national systems and capacities at 
every level. This includes support for policy and legal 
frameworks, institutional development, public finance 
and service delivery. Joint monitoring, periodic reviews 
and evaluations are built into the framework, using 
national indicators where possible, and aligned to SDG 
reporting. The UN will also leverage its local presence, 
regional reach and global networks to bring relevant 
knowledge, innovation and partnerships. It will support 
the Government to connect with regional platforms, share 
solutions across borders and apply global norms and 
standards in a way that fits the national context. 
The UN will also prioritize strengthening national ownership 
and capacity, recognizing the growing pressures on official 
development assistance. It will support the development 
of sustainability plans that enable national and local 
institutions to maintain, expand and drive results beyond 
the life cycle of the Cooperation Framework, including 
through joint and complementary initiatives with national 
industrial institutions and development banks. Inclusive 
and transparent accountability mechanisms will be 
promoted, engaging citizens, Parliament, civil society and 
development partners. These combined efforts will help 
ensure that progress is measured, shared and sustained, 
with lasting impact for people and communities.

402.7 Leaving No One Behind
In Uganda, several groups remain at risk of being left 
behind. These include women and girls, ethnic minorities 
and Indigenous peoples, peoples with disabilities, people 
living with HIV, refugees, asylum seekers, migrants and 
the working poor, particularly youth and children and 
other minority groups. Geographic isolation is putting 
communities in Karamoja, West Nile, mountain regions, 
islands and forest-adjacent settlements at further 
risk. The overall exclusion of those at risk of being 
left behind is driven by structural challenges, such as 
weak enforcement of protective laws, under-resourced 
institutions, poor infrastructure and vulnerability to 
shocks including such as conflict, climate change and 
economic crises. Multidimensional poverty and inequality 
cut across these groups, reinforcing cycles of deprivation 
and limiting access to essential services, opportunities 
and decision-making. Addressing these intersecting 
challenges is central to advancing inclusive development 
and fulfilling the pledge to leave no one behind.
‘Leave No One Behind’ is more than a guiding principle in 
this Cooperation Framework; it is a stand-alone outcome 
with dedicated outputs that focus on tackling the drivers 
of exclusion and inequality in Uganda. This directly 
supports Uganda’s Vision 2040 and the country’s bold 
ambition to become an inclusive, just and prosperous 
society. It also aligns with the core aim of the Parish 
Development Model, which seeks to lift the 39 per cent of 
Ugandans still outside the money economy by delivering 
targeted support at the household level. Outcome 3 
of the Framework takes this determination forward 
by focusing on ending gender-based discrimination, 
dismantling structural barriers and ensuring that people 
with disabilities and other underserved groups live with 
dignity and equal opportunity.
Using gender-transformative and human rights-based 
approaches across all programming, the UN’s contribution 
under Outcome 3 will focus on addressing discriminatory 
norms, strengthening legal protection and improving 
national systems to deliver inclusive and equitable services. 
The UN will work with the Government to ensure that the 
most excluded are visible in national data, heard in policy 
spaces, and protected under the law. Interventions will 
target both the formal systems for education, health and 
justice and the informal practices that sustain exclusion. 
The aim is not just to close gaps, but to balance power and 
expand opportunity in a way that is lasting and owned by 
communities. By making this a dedicated outcome, the 
Cooperation Framework reinforces the UN’s commitment 
to support Uganda in realizing its vision: one where no 
one is left behind, whether by geography, gender, disability, 
poverty or any other form of exclusion.
2.8 United Nations Country Team Configuration
The UN Country Team (UNCT) in Uganda consists of the 
UN system’s funds, programmes, specialized agencies, 
departments and offices and related UN system entities 
that support the country either through physical presence 
or remotely. The UNCT configuration demonstrates the 
individual and collective strength of technical expertise, 
knowledge and experience of the UN system to deliver on 
the Cooperation Framework commitments in support of 
Uganda’s development agenda. The current composition 
of 29 entities is expanding to 32 in 2026, with the addition 
of four entities and loss of one. The United Nations 
Office of Counter-Terrorism (UNOCT), ITU, the UN Office 
on South-South and Triangular Cooperation, and the UN 
Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies will add to 
the UN footprint in Uganda while the International Atomic 
Energy Agency will not be part of the new Cooperation 
Framework. These additional capacities will ensure the 
UN responds more effectively to emerging priorities, 
including digital transformation, regional security and 
cybergovernance. 
The UNCT brings a mix of operational, policy, normative 
and coordination expertise, with agencies supporting 
both upstream reform and downstream delivery. This 
diversity of mandates and technical depth means 
the UN is well placed to deliver integrated solutions 
across the Cooperation Framework’s six outcomes. The 
configuration is also increasingly agile, with more joint 
programming, pooled resources and multi-agency teams 
supporting Government priorities at national and subnational levels.

The Pact for the Future and six SDG transitions – food

Cooperation Framework aligns with one or more of these 
transitions and collectively addresses Uganda’s strategic 
priorities under Vision 2040 and NDP IV. By linking national 
development goals to global pathways for acceleration, 
the Cooperation Framework provides a solid platform for 
advancing the 2030 Agenda in Uganda.
The UN system in Uganda will adopt a joined-up approach 
that brings different agencies together under one plan, 
with shared goals and collective accountability. This 
Cooperation Framework will prioritize joint programmes, 
catalytic investments and demonstration initiatives 
that are scalable, replicable and responsive to national 
needs. These initiatives will be co-created with the

national ownership and alignment with national planning

particularly in areas such as rehabilitation, reintegration

The Cooperation Framework represents a core shift, 
placing data, digital transformation, foresight and 
innovation at the centre of delivery. The UN will use global 
expertise, regional capabilities and local networks to unlock 
systemic change and address complex challenges. The 
Cooperation Framework emphasizes integrated planning

The Cooperation Framework will reinforce national

enable more adaptive programming and promote mutual 
reinforcement across sectors.
3.2 Cooperation Framework Governance, Accountability and 
Coordination
The Cooperation Framework will be governed by a 
Government-UN Joint Steering Committee, co-chaired 
by the Office of the Prime Minister and the UN Resident 
Coordinator. This committee provides strategic 
oversight, advice on alignment with national priorities 
and endorsement of annual performance reviews. 
Membership includes representatives from key ministries, 
UN agencies and civil society.
The Joint Steering Committee will be supported by the 
Deputies Group, a horizontal management layer providing 
technical guidance across results areas. It will advise on 
policy coherence, ensure responsiveness to the national 
context and support implementation monitoring. The 
Joint Steering Committee and Deputies Group will link 
directly to planning and results of structures within the 
Cooperation Framework.
3.3 Cooperation Framework Internal 
Management Structure

Groups, one for each Cooperation Framework outcome. 
Each group is co-led by a UN entity and a relevant government 
institution. The Outcome Result Group leaders will oversee 
planning, delivery and monitoring of joint workplans and 
coordinate the development of joint programmes. Each 
group is complemented by the Results-Based Management 
or the Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL) Group and 
the UN Communications and Partnerships Group.
The Operations Management Team will continue to 
lead operational efficiency and implementation of the 
Business Operations Strategy, while thematic groups 
on human rights, gender equality, disability inclusion 
and youth will provide technical advice to the Outcome 
Results Groups and the UNCT.

of a country’s development context, undertaken in 
close collaboration with the Government and other 
stakeholders. In Uganda, the Country Analysis guides 
the implementation of the Cooperation Framework, with 
its findings shaping strategic focus, transformational 
change and impact. It draws on national data sources, 
such as the 2024 Census, the Voluntary National Review 
as well as the Cooperation Framework 2021-25 evaluation 
and the NDP IV. The CA process is broad, evidencebased and inclusive, actively engaging the Government, 
development partners, civil society, academia and the 
UN system. Multiple analytic approaches will be applied 
including futures and foresight techniques and root cause 
and rights-based analyses. 
To ensure agility, the analysis will be updated annually, 
with new data and emerging trends including regional and 
cross-border dimensions. The updated CA will continue 
shaping the Cooperation Framework through its annual 
joint work plans. The final report undergoes rigorous 
review by the UN Country Team, the Government and the 
UN Development Coordination Office to ensure currency, 
credibility and responsiveness to evolving national 
context.
4.2 Monitoring Plan
Monitoring of the Cooperation Framework is framed 
around its robust results framework, which details 
baselines, targets and key performance indicators for all 
outcomes and outputs, directly aligned with relevant SDG 
indicators. Each indicator has designated UN entities 
responsible for routine data collection, ensuring clear 
accountability. All people centric indicators and data will 
be disaggregated as much as possible with mandatory 
sex, age and disability disaggregation. The UNCT will 
apply the System-Wide Action Plan (SWAP) Gender 
Scorecard to monitor gender integration and ensure risks 
of backlash against and/or erosion of women’s rights 
are systematically mitigated. Adaptive risk monitoring 
will enable timely adjustments in response to emerging 
challenges. Annual gender reviews will be conducted, and 
children, disability and gender performance indicators 
will be embedded in the joint workplan to track gender 
equality and women’s empowerment progress across all 
outcomes.

4.2.1. Risks and Opportunities 
The Cooperation Framework is implemented within a 
complex landscape of interconnected risks, as outlined 
in the Country Analysis, that may impede progress 
towards the SDGs. These multidimensional challenges 
span political, governance, environmental, economic 
and social domains and often reinforce one another. 
Key risks include potential instability associated with 
political transitions and the marginalization of youth; 
governance gaps that contribute to corruption and 
undermine public trust and respect for human rights; 
environmental degradation driven by climate change and 
unsustainable resource use; and economic vulnerabilities 
linked to aid dependency and inflation. Deep-rooted 
social inequalities, particularly those affecting women, 
youth and other underserved groups, continue to erode 
social cohesion and hinder human development. Based 
on historical patterns, the 2026 general elections also 
present a significant risk of violence. Moreover, dwindling 
resources and a contracting civic space pose serious 
threats to effective programme implementation and the 
realization of the SDGs.
To navigate this landscape, the UN development system 
will employ an integrated and adaptive approach. 
Mitigation strategies are embedded within the Cooperation 
Framework’s design, focusing on strengthening 
accountable institutions, promoting inclusive economic 
opportunities, fostering social cohesion and human 
rights, and building climate resilience. The UN will 
strategically invest in civic education and stakeholder 
engagement, including security organs, to safeguard 
national programmes.
The UN will utilize its monitoring system for continuous 
risk analysis and adaptive management. Data from joint 
reviews and the UN INFO platform will enable regular 
scanning of the context, allowing the UNCT to proactively 
adjust programming in response to emerging threats. 
This flexible approach presents an opportunity not only 
to manage risks but to strategically intervene to break 
negative cycles, turning vulnerabilities into pathways for 
resilient and sustainable development.
4.2.2. Cooperation Framework Review
and Reporting 
To ensure agility, the UN Country Analysis will undergo an 
annual light update (between September and December) 
by a designated inter-agency team, tracking key indicators 
via a dashboard. Building on this, the Outcome Results 
Groups, in collaboration with government partners, 
will conduct light annual reviews of the Cooperation 
Framework. These reviews will assess the continued 
relevance of the theory of change and the measurability 
of the results framework. The annual reviews will also 
provide a formal platform for all stakeholders to take 
stock of progress against agreed-upon results, address 
challenges and make necessary adjustments.
For reporting, Outcome Results Groups will perform quarterly 
data updates on the UN INFO platform. These updates 
facilitate the compilation of the annual One UN Country 
Results Report, which will be presented to the Joint Steering 
Committee for approval each March. Crucially, findings 
from the report will provide consolidated, evidence-based 
contributions to the Government’s programme reports on 
the NDP IV and inform the preparation of Uganda’s Voluntary 
National Reviews, ensuring Cooperation Framework’s full 
alignment with national priorities and reporting cycles.
To enhance evidence-based planning, decision-making and 
accountability, the Cooperation Framework will promote 
the integration of digital tools into national and sectoral 
M&E systems. This includes support for the development 
and scaling of real-time data platforms, interactive digital 
dashboards and AI-enabled analytics that can improve 
timeliness, accuracy and granularity of data used for policy 
and programmatic decisions. These innovations will enable 
national institutions and development partners to track 
progress on SDG targets more effectively, identify emerging 
trends and adapt interventions in a timely manner. The UN 
will work closely with government counterparts to strengthen 
the capacity of national statistical and M&E systems to 
leverage these technologies, ensuring interoperability and 
data quality and inclusive access to digital M&E solutions.
4.3 Evaluation Plan
The UNCT will commission a mandatory, independent 
final evaluation of the Cooperation Framework in its 
penultimate year, 2029. This summative evaluation 
will be informed by the findings of preceding UN entity 
country programme evaluations, thematic evaluations 
and joint programme reviews, which will be timed and 
sequenced accordingly to provide a robust evidence
base.
Conducted by external consultants, the evaluation will 
be managed under the oversight of a multi-stakeholder 
Evaluation Steering Committee. The entire process 
will strictly adhere to United Nations Evaluation Group 
norms and standards, guaranteeing quality, credibility 
and independence. Key stakeholders, including the 
Government of Uganda, civil society, private sector, 
academia and programme beneficiaries, will be actively 
engaged throughout the evaluation process to ensure a 
comprehensive and inclusive assessment that informs 
the subsequent programming cycle.

The programme will be nationally executed under the 
overall coordination of the Office of the Prime Minister 
(the Government Coordinating Authority). The Cooperation 
Framework will be made operational through the 
development of joint work plan(s) and/or agency-specific 
workplans and project documents, as necessary, which 
describe the specific results to be achieved and will form 
an agreement between the UN system agencies and 
each Implementing Partner, as necessary, on the use of 
resources. To the extent possible the UN system agencies 
and partners will use the minimum documents necessary, 
namely the signed Cooperation Framework and signed joint 
or agency-specific workplans and project documents to 
implement programmatic initiatives. However, as necessary 
and appropriate, project documents can be prepared using, 
inter alia, the relevant text from the Cooperation Framework 
and joint or agency-specific workplans and/or project 
documents. 
Cash assistance for travel, stipends, honorariums and other 
costs shall be set at rates commensurate with those applied 
in the country, but not higher than those applicable to the 
United Nations system (as stated in the International Civil 
Service Commission circulars).
2. Programme Implementation 
(HACT) 
 All cash transfers to an Implementing Partner are based on 
the Work Plans (WPs)[3] agreed between the Implementing 
Partner and the UN system agencies. Cash transfers for 
activities detailed in WP scan be made by the UN system 
agencies using the following modalities:
1. Cash transferred directly to the Implementing 
Partner: 
A. Prior to the start of activities (direct cash 
transfer), or 
B. After activities have been completed 
(reimbursement). 
2. Direct payment to vendors or third parties for 
obligations incurred by the Implementing Partners 
on the basis of requests signed by the designated 
official of the Implementing Partner.
3. Direct payments to vendors or third parties for 
obligations incurred by UN system agencies in 
support of activities agreed with Implementing 
Partners. 
Where cash transfers are made to the national institution, 
the national institution shall transfer such cash promptly to 
the Implementing Partner.
Direct cash transfers shall be requested and released 
for programme implementation periods not exceeding 
three months. Reimbursements of previously authorized 
expenditures shall be requested and released quarterly or 
after the completion of activities. The UN system agencies 
shall not be obligated to reimburse expenditure made by 
the Implementing Partner over and above the authorized 
amounts.
Following the completion of any activity, any balance 
of funds shall be refunded or programmed by mutual 
agreement between the Implementing Partner and the UN 
system agencies.
Cash transfer modalities, the size of disbursements and the 
scope and frequency of assurance activities may depend on 
the findings of a review of the public financial management 
capacity in the case of a government Implementing Partner 
and of an assessment of the financial management 
capacity of the non-UN[4] Implementing Partner. A qualified 
consultant, such as a public accounting firm, selected by 
the UN system agencies may conduct such an assessment, 
in which the Implementing Partner shall participate. The 
Implementing Partner may participate in the selection of the 
consultant.

3. Mobilizing Resources for the 
Cooperation Framework
The UN system agencies will provide support to the 
development and implementation of activities within the 
Cooperation Framework, which may include technical 
support, cash assistance, supplies, commodities and 
equipment, procurement services, transport, funds for 
advocacy, research and studies, consultancies, programme 
development, monitoring and evaluation, training activities 
and staff support. Part of the UN system entities’ support 
may be provided to non-governmental [and civil society] 
organizations as agreed within the framework of the 
individual workplans and project documents.
Additional support may include access to UN organizationmanaged global information systems, the network of 
the UN system agencies’ country offices and specialized 
information systems, including rosters of consultants 
and providers of development services and access to the 
support provided by the network of UN specialized agencies, 
funds and programmes. The UN system agencies shall 
appoint staff and consultants for programme development, 
programme support, technical assistance, as well as 
monitoring and evaluation activities.
Subject to annual reviews and progress in the implementation 
of the programme, the UN system agencies’ funds are 
distributed by calendar year and in accordance with the 
Cooperation Framework. These budgets will be reviewed 
and further detailed in the workplans and project documents. 
By mutual consent between the Government and the UN 
development system entities, funds not earmarked by 
donors to UN development system agencies for specific 
activities may be re-allocated to other programmatically 
equally worthwhile activities.
The Government will support the UN system agencies’ 
efforts to raise funds required to meet the needs of this 
Cooperation Framework and will cooperate with the UN 
system agencies including: encouraging potential donor 
governments to make available to the UN system agencies 
the funds needed to implement unfunded components of the 
programme; endorsing the UN system agencies’ efforts to 
raise funds for the programme from other sources, including 
the private sector both internationally and in Uganda and by 
permitting contributions from individuals, corporations and 
foundations in Uganda to support this programme which 
will be tax exempt for the donor, to the maximum extent 
permissible under applicable law.
4. Cooperation Framework 
Monitoring and Evaluation
Implementing Partners agree to cooperate with the UN 
system agencies for monitoring all activities supported by 
cash transfers and will facilitate access to relevant financial 
records and personnel responsible for the administration of 
cash provided by the UN system agencies. To that effect, 
Implementing Partners agree to the following:
1. Periodic on-site reviews and spot checks of their 
financial records by the UN system agencies 
or their representatives, as appropriate, and as 
described in specific clauses of their engagement 
documents/ contracts with the UN system 
agencies.
2. Programmatic monitoring of activities following the 
UN system agencies’ standards and guidance for 
site visits and field monitoring.
Special or scheduled audits: Each UN organization, in 
collaboration with other UN system agencies (where so 
desired and in consultation with the respective coordinating 
Ministry) will establish an annual audit plan, giving priority to 
audits of Implementing Partners with large amounts of cash 
assistance provided by the UN system agencies and those 
whose financial management capacity needs strengthening.
